newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters bolster support for striking members.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters bolster support for striking members.

text.p: The Teamsters union scrambled to set up food banks, financial assistance and other support programs nationwide on Thursday as United Parcel Service strikers prepared to go without paychecks for the first time in the 11-day-old walkout.

Teamster locals from Maine to California met with representatives of community organizations such as credit unions, United Way agencies and other charities in hopes of offering a full range of social services to striking members and their families.
Food banks, clothing drives, credit assistance programs and counseling groups were expected to begin springing up across the country.

Union locals also operated their own job fairs in hopes of finding work for strikers. Some of the calls for temporary workers have come from trucking companies inundated with new business because of the strike.
Teamster officials said most of the 185,000 workers on strike at UPS would not need assistance for some time.

"We've been telling our people to prepare for this contract -- we never said prepare for a strike -- but be prepared financially. Don't go out and buy your new truck this summer. Don't go buy your new house this summer," said Paul Lovinus, an official with Teamsters Local 344 in Milwaukee.
On Friday, the strike was to pass a disturbing milestone for Teamsters, as their weekly paycheck is replaced by the first disbursement of $55-a-week strike benefit.

"Fifty-five dollars is better than zero. But it won't help anybody pay bills. One of the things we're working on real hard is a service to help members in dire need, like when they're in danger of having their lights turned off," said Marion Ray, a Teamster official in Atlanta.
Although some Teamster members have decided to cross picket lines, there have been few signs of weakness among those who are striking over pay, benefits and job security.
"As long as it takes. I have money in the bank. I have a strong family, a big family that supports me 100 percent," 16-year UPS veteran Agustin Novo said outside a company facility in Hialeah, Fla.
"I think a lot of us prepared for this. We've been saying for a long time, 'Put a little bit away, put a little bit away,'" the father of two added.
But Teamster officials said most strikers will not begin to feel the pinch until next month's bills start coming due.
"That's when you're making partial payments on all your bills," Milwaukee Teamster official Lovinus.
It is for that day that Teamster locals have begun to prepare.
In some parts of the country, the union has mailed out invitations to explore the services of local credit unions which have a long relationship with the Teamsters.

Strikers also have been given advice on how to approach banks and other creditors about payments on mortgages and car loans. Union officials said lenders so far have been "fairly decent" about giving strikers an extra 30-60 days to make payments.
The Teamsters were talking to other labor organizations, including the AFL-CIO, about ways to organize emergency funds for strikers and their families.
In Atlanta, Teamster Local 728 has also been able to place strikers with unionized trucking companies whose shipping volumes have skyrocketed because of the strike.

"A lot of freight companies have been calling in and saying, look, these volumes are just so demanding. They know UPS people are hard-working and they know the system," Teamster organizer John Wayne Garrett said.
One of those carriers, Borg Warner subsidiary Pony Express Delivery Service, announced a 50 percent rise in volume nationwide due to the UPS strike.
